Why Collectible Figures looks calm as a whole category. This category holds 12 different topics. A few of them, Star Wars, Disney, and Marvel figures, plus generic action figures, are growing fast. Filter the table below to Collectible Figures to see this for yourself.

Reading this dashboard. Google gives us 4 years of history, so we can compare this month to the same month last year (that's "year over year"). TikTok only gives us the last 12 months, not enough for that comparison, so year over year only shows up for Google. Month over month and quarter over quarter work everywhere since they need less history.

Translations. The English column is a plain translation. Brand names like Labubu, Pop Mart, Jellycat, and Lego are kept as-is since people search for them the same way in both languages.

Missing data. A few topics only have TikTok numbers because Google doesn't have enough searches to measure. Two topics (classic Mickey Mouse and classic merchandise) have no usable data from either source and are left out of the totals.
Summary
This page answers three simple questions: what are people talking about right now, which of those topics actually look set to keep growing, and where should you focus next.
What people are discussing, by category
Specific products and collaborations that suddenly got a lot more searches last month.
Topics with potential to become significant trends
These aren't just up right now, a forecasting model expects them to keep growing over the next 3 to 6 months.
Investment potential, in four groups
Everything above, sorted into what to act on, what to watch, what to hold onto, and what's cooling down.
Which categories are actually growing. Collectible Figures is the only category growing broadly right now, not just because of one hot product. Trading Cards has grown the most over the past year, even with a quieter last few months. Every other category (Art Toys, Plush, Educational, Vintage, Dolls) is down compared to a year ago, even when one specific product inside it is doing well. That matters when deciding if something is a real category shift or just one lucky product.

How to read the four groups. "Act now" and "Watch" both come from a forecasting model that expects more growth, the difference is how confident the model is in its own prediction. "Harvest" means a topic already grew and should hold onto those gains, but probably won't grow much further. "Cooling" means a topic looks great in the recent numbers, but the model expects it to fall back, something you'd miss if you only looked at last month's percentage.

Why Collectible Figures looks calm as a whole category. Four of the topics here, Star Wars, Disney, Marvel, and generic action figures, all sit inside Collectible Figures. But that category's overall growth number looks much smaller, because it also contains other topics that are flat or shrinking, which cancel out the fast-growing ones.

How this list is chosen. Only topics that are genuinely growing on every measure shown here make this list, not just one good month.
New trends, last month
Specific search phrases, not the 96 main topics, that jumped the most last month. This is usually where something new shows up first, before it becomes an official trend.
How to read this. These are raw search phrases, so they catch things a fixed topic list would miss: brand collaborations, new product types, viral moments. A few highlights: Squishmallow x McDonald's Happy Meal showed up across five different searches at once on both Google and TikTok, a much stronger signal than any single spike. "Hirono adalah" ("what is Hirono") suggests growing curiosity about that Pop Mart character, maybe a new release. Boneka porselen (porcelain dolls) confirms a trend we also saw elsewhere in this dashboard.

A word of caution. This data isn't manually checked, so a few results can be false alarms, generic phrases that happen to include a tracked word (for example, football-related "kartu" results, "kartu" means "card" in Indonesian, have been removed). Use this tab to explore ideas, not as a finished conclusion.
Where's this heading
A forecasting model, not just last month's number, predicts where each topic is heading next. The most reliable predictions come first.

How this works. Each topic's full history of Google searches (up to 4 years) is fed into a forecasting model that predicts the next 6 months. Accelerating means the model expects it to keep climbing. Holding gains means it already grew, but the model expects it to level off rather than keep growing. Pulling back means the model expects it to shrink back toward its older level. Too volatile to forecast means the model wasn't confident enough in its own prediction, so we show that honestly instead of hiding it.

Why some topics aren't forecast at all. TikTok only has 12 months of history, too short for a reliable forecast. So this page only forecasts topics with enough Google history. A few well-known topics (Lego, Funko Pop, Labubu, Pop Mart, Sonny Angel) aren't forecast because their recent pattern already tells the story clearly.
All keywords, modeled
Every search term we found, 4,553 of them, each with a quick forecast for the next 3 months. This uses a faster, simpler method than the detailed forecasts above, so treat it as a rough guide rather than the final word.
Search term Category Source Latest / mo MoM Modeled trend +3mo forecast Detailed forecast?
How this works. For each search term, we look at its last 6 months and draw a trend line through it, then use that line to guess the next 3 months. We test the method by hiding the most recent month and checking if it would have guessed right. This is much quicker than the detailed forecasts above, which is why it can run on thousands of terms at once, but it can miss seasonal patterns or sudden changes, treat it as a first pass, not the final word.
